title: Savitri's vow
hookLine: in the forest hermitage Savitri counts the days nobody else is counting, and keeps a hard vrata before the last one
carry: a vrata is a vow kept with the body

cards: A calendar, kept in one person's head. In the forest hermitage, nobody else is counting. Satyavan gathers fruit and splits wood.
His father, a king who lost his sight and then his kingdom, lives there quietly with his wife. Savitri has put away her jewels and wears the rough clothing of the forest.
She serves the old couple and speaks gently to everyone. And every day, she counts. The sage Narada said at her father's court that Satyavan would not live out the year.
She tells no one. In the epic, those words stay with her day and night.

teach.b: As the day draws close, Savitri takes a vow. The epic calls it the triratra, the three-night vow, and she keeps it standing, without food, day and night. Her father-in-law, Dyumatsena, calls it too hard.
Savitri answers gently: don't grieve, father. It's resolve that carries a vow through. And the old king, blind and kind, gives way: keep it, then.
She doesn't tell him why. She takes the fear she has carried alone and offers it, with her own body.

teach.h: A VRATA: A VOW KEPT WITH THE BODY.
teach.b: That's a vrata: a vow kept with discipline, often by fasting, offered to God for a purpose. It's one of the most lived parts of Hinduism.

teach.h: A FAST IN MANY HOMES THIS WEEK.
teach.b: Ekadashi fasts, Monday fasts for Shiva, Navaratri fasts: in many Hindu homes, someone is keeping one this week. Tradition says steady discipline like this gathers tapas, a strength that comes from holding firm.
And Savitri's vow has a living descendant.

Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep the Vat Savitri vrata: they fast, wind thread around a banyan tree, and hear this very story, praying for their husbands' long lives.
On the last night Savitri stands until morning. Then the day itself arrives. She makes her offerings to the fire, and the hermits bless her.
The elders urge her to eat at last.

teach.h: I'LL EAT WHEN THE SUN GOES DOWN.
teach.b: She says she'll eat when the sun goes down. For today: a vrata isn't a diet or a punishment. It's love and resolve, kept in the body and offered.

how: In the epic, Savitri keeps her three-night vow standing and fasting just before the day Narada foretold; the Vat Savitri vrata, kept each year by many married Hindu women in the month of Jyeshtha, recalls her story.

games.q: your nani is keeping an ekadashi fast, and your friend says it's 'basically a diet.' by Savitri's story, what's a vrata?

a vow kept with the body and offered to God, like Savitri's three nights.
games.why: Savitri's fast wasn't about food. it was love and resolve, kept in the body and offered. that's a vrata.

practice: A vrata usually begins with a sankalpa, a short spoken intention. Stand if you can, or sit tall.

Bring to mind one person or one need you'd like to offer something for, and make a tiny sankalpa in your own words: what you'll keep, for how long, and for whom; a meal without your phone, a kind word you won't skip.
If you pray, offer it to God; if not, hold it as a promise to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Vrata, a vow kept with the body. Savitri's three nights, standing, live on in a vrata women still keep every year.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a vow, often kept with fasting; Savitri's is a three-night one.
